b: On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform. She had starved herself to death. Charlene had never been diagnosed with anorexia, not because her self-starvation went unnoticed, but because the diagnosis, in its Western form, was mostly unknown in the East. Her death changed that overnight. Splashed across the front pages were stark headlines such as ‘Girl Who Died In Street Was A Walking Skeleton’.

Local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and quickly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it. The ideas spread rapidly – particularly that anorexia involved distorted self-perceptions about one’s body (dysmorphia) and an intense, borderline delusional, fear of gaining weight, often cued by prevailing beauty standards (notably, a cultural fixation with slender female bodies). Mass public education campaigns followed. Hotlines opened, celebrities spoke out. Anorexia became part of the zeitgeist.

Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees. Most of these women did not obsess over their bodies, nor fear becoming fat. They instead complained of somatic (bodily) ailments: uncomfortable bloating, a profound lack of appetite. The cognitive hallmark of Western anorexia – a distorted body image – was largely absent. Lee seemed to be documenting a distinct form of self-starvation with its own local logic. The situation has changed dramatically since then. By 2007, more than three-quarters of the anorexic patients Lee treated cited ‘fat phobia’ as a central motivation. Today, anorexia in Hong Kong is terrifyingly common, affecting roughly one in 200 schoolgirls – comparable to trends in the United States.

We do not know the form that Charlene’s illness took. What we do know is that her death became a catalyst for the rapid importation of a Western conceptual framework that reshaped how Hong Kong understood and experienced disordered eating in young women.

Anorexia is just one example from a compendium of curious cases in which culture seemingly shapes mental disorders. For example, anthropologists have documented how cultures sculpt ‘idioms of distress’ – socially learned and sanctioned ways of communicating unusual mental episodes and patterns of psychological suffering. Hallucinations and dissociative states are routinely interpreted as forms of spiritual possession across the globe, as with Zār in northeast Africa and the Middle East.

These cases are not fringe oddities. Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears. In China, patients who meet Western criteria for depression present mainly with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, insomnia and headaches, rather than psychological symptoms, like low self-esteem and apathy. Delusions, multiple personality and social anxiety also take different forms in different cultures.

Cultural variation in psychiatry raises fundamental and increasingly urgent questions about abnormal minds. What precisely can culture shape? We usually think of mental disorder as something going wrong inside a person, and of culture as shaping how that internal problem is expressed and socially understood. Can culture penetrate deeper, to reshape the internal problem itself? What would that even look like?

The suggestion that cultural variables can significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental disorders, including brute neurobiological hardware, may seem counterintuitive, even radical. But I’ll make the case that culture may possess a more substantial ability to do so – in some disorders, to some degrees – than is generally acknowledged. The basic reason is that the brain, the organ of the mind, is plastic and has functions of representing and adapting to a rich social world.

This could well allow cultural ecosystems to inculcate ‘local’ kinds of disorders – ones that may look similar to their cross-cultural counterparts, but differ in their psychological and even neurological profiles in ways consequential for scientific classification and treatment. ‘Anorexia’ or ‘depression’ in one cultural context may then be best understood as a different condition altogether in another. Mental disorders are already notoriously heterogeneous: one study of 3,703 patients diagnosed with depression found 1,030 distinct combinations of symptoms. One source of this variation may be cultural environments, including subcultures within a country’s borders. These possibilities hinge on unsettled questions about how plastic the mechanisms of mental disorders really are, and whether cultural factors have the right kind of causal access to them.

To begin, let me distinguish three widely accepted ways that culture can shape mental disorders, before investigating whether it can also shape their internal mechanisms. When I say ‘culture’, I mean a broad class of sociocultural factors, including social roles, norms, values, institutional and political structures, even particular medical beliefs and practices. By ‘shape’, I mean causally influence.
Hearing God speak seems a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals cultivate the experience

The first widely accepted way is by shaping our concepts of disorder. Here I am accepting a basic distinction between our various concepts of mental disorder (including lay and scientific theories of what disorders are, and what explains them), and the actual nature of those conditions. Historians have long shown that psychiatric concepts can be covertly shaped by social forces. What counts as ‘normal’ versus ‘eccentric’ versus ‘pathological’ behaviour is often prescribed by prevailing cultural norms and scientific authorities (whether legitimate or pseudo). A particularly dramatic example from 1851 is the diagnosis ‘Drapetomania’, which was given exclusively to Black slaves who fled their captors. The warped logic – which rested on the widespread and pernicious belief that God had ordained Black people to be enslaved – was that slavery was so beneficial, only a mentally ill person would cut and run. In this case, the concept was culturally shaped and pseudo, because it did not refer to a genuine condition, only mentally competent agents acting rationally.

But culture can legitimately inform psychiatric concepts, such as notions of harm and thresholds for ‘appropriate’ behaviour. Answers to questions like How much despondence or apathy is pathological? and Is this person’s gambling significantly interfering with their life? are partly scientific and partly cultural. For example, hearing God speak seems like a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals actively cultivate the experience and consider it a sign of closeness to God. Psychiatry’s own guidelines recognise that such experiences can be a normal part of religious life.

The second accepted form of cultural shaping is by modulating mental health outcomes, through various pathways, including the social determinants of health. Poverty, discrimination, social isolation, stigma and access to care comprise psychosocial risk factors that can significantly impact disorder prevalence, treatment success, even mortality rates. For example, migrants and their children develop schizophrenia at three times the rate of native-born populations, a gap that researchers have linked to discrimination and social exclusion.

The third way involves culture shaping the lived experience of mental disorder. Medical anthropologists distinguish between a ‘disease’ – a biological pathology that explains medical symptoms – and an ‘illness’ – how the symptoms of disease are experienced, expressed and socially understood. Culture can significantly shape illness. For example, an HIV infection may be the same disease everywhere, but the experience of AIDS (the late stage of the HIV infection) can differ considerably across cultural contexts – eg, where there is widespread belief that AIDS is a form of divine punishment.

The changing form of self-starvation in Hong Kong is commonly explained as an interaction of two of those types of cultural shaping. First, a Western theory of anorexia reshaped the concept of anorexia in Hong Kong, as understood by both clinicians and laypeople. Second, that conceptual uptake induced new ways of understanding, experiencing and expressing anorexic distress, thereby producing new symptoms. Culture shaped medical concepts; concepts shaped illness. The philosopher Ian Hacking argued that this situation can create a complex feedback loop, where concepts and illness-experience continuously remake each other. In The Social Construction of What? (1999), he called this the ‘looping effect’.

Can culture penetrate deeper, to shape diseases themselves? By shaping disease, I mean creating new pathologies, or altering an existing one enough that it becomes a new condition, one we must classify, explain and treat differently. In somatic medicine, the answer is generally ‘no’ for culture, but ‘yes’ for chemical and biological factors. If we expose a case of tuberculosis to antibiotics, it can evolve inside a patient into multidrug-resistant TB, which calls for a distinct diagnosis and treatment strategy. Environmental toxins, genetic mutations, infections and diet can all reshape pathologies. Cultural variables may play an upstream role, for example, by disposing doctors to overprescribe antibiotics. But the cultural content – the beliefs and meanings behind such practices – makes no difference to the disease itself. Culture seems to lack the right sort of causal connection to underlying pathologies.

A crisp distinction between ‘illness’ and ‘disease’ seems appropriate for most somatic disorders: cholera, cancer and cirrhosis are the same diseases whether they appear in Beijing or Boston, even if illness profiles can vary wildly. Does the distinction hold for psychiatry?

There are two reasons to suspect it does not. First, the paradigmatic features of mental disorders – abnormal thoughts, feelings, behaviours – overlap massively with features of illness, which can be shaped by culture. A cardiologist does not consult their patient’s beliefs to diagnose or explain a leaking heart valve. But psychiatrists make diagnoses based on mental ‘signs’ (outwardly observable behaviours, like disorganised speech) and ‘symptoms’ (self-reports about lived experience, such as low self-esteem or a fear of fatness). These features are also thought to partially explain disorders: in anorexia, a fear of fatness is sometimes thought to drive self-starvation.

Second, it is not obvious that mental disorders depend on biological diseases, at least in the familiar medical sense. There is no identified pathophysiology for anorexia, depression, schizophrenia or any other mental disorder – no clear account of system dysfunction, no ‘chemical imbalance’. The picture instead is far messier: the brains and bodies of mentally ill people differ from unafflicted populations in myriad subtle ways. Psychiatry is left with diverse theories of disorder pitched at different explanatory levels – some plausible, all partial and piecemeal, none yet mature enough to revolutionise our understanding.
Mental software is not cleanly separable from its neural hardware

Even so, psychiatric institutions conceptualise mental conditions as disease-like. The American Psychiatric Association (APA), which writes and publishes the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), defines mental disorder as a pattern of disturbance reflecting ‘a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning’ – a ‘dysfunction in the individual’. More daringly, the National Institute of Mental Health’s (NIMH) research framework explicitly formulates mental disorders as ‘disorders of brain circuits’.

What’s going on here? The APA and NIMH are making an empirical bet that disease-like explanations will earn their keep in psychiatry, once we’ve learned all we want to know about the mind and its maladies. That is, they assume there are deeper internal structures that explain why signs and symptoms tend to hang together. This need not amount to a crude biological reductionism; the relevant structures need not be hidden brain diseases. But the brain’s ability to process information – which supports thinking, feeling and acting – is inextricably entangled with its physiological functions. Mental software is not cleanly separable from its neural hardware.

We need a general term for the internal structures that might explain why symptoms hang together. Let’s call them ‘neurocomputational mechanisms’, or NCMs for short. ‘Neuro’ plus ‘computational’ means these mechanisms could be described at the neural level, the information-processing level, or both.

For example, some specific phobias are thought to depend on a learned threat-association that stubbornly resists updating. Phobic responses are characteristically sticky: arachnophobia can persist despite the patient earnestly believing that spiders are harmless and wanting to tame their fear. The mechanism sustaining that association would be an NCM: an internal structure that partly controls the excessive fear responses and avoidance behaviours typical of phobias. Phobias are usually treatable by exposure therapy, which is thought to work on that mechanism by supplying new learning that overpowers the original, obstinate association.

One view – let’s call it ‘universalism’ – assumes that the NCMs relevant to psychopathology are culturally invariant. In conceptualising disorders as disease-like, the DSM and NIMH view them as breakdowns in a shared bio-psycho human nature, insulated against cultural influence. Universalism thinks of mental disorders like hydrangeas, which take on different forms in different environments. A hydrangea growing in acidic soil rich with aluminium blooms sky-blue flowers; in chalky soil, its flowers are pastel pink. But it is still the same plant, with the same internal pigment, moulded by interactions with its ecosystem. In this, universalism preserves a crisp distinction between illness and underlying NCMs that fix a disorder’s scientific identity.

In contrast, the view I want to develop – call it ‘deep shaping’ – accepts the distinction between illness and the underlying NCMs, but hypothesises that culture can causally shape both (to some degree, in some cases).

This deep-shaping picture is importantly different from a social constructionism about mental disorder. As I’ll use the term, social constructionism is the view that a mental disorder can be almost fully explained by social factors, with no need to posit internal mechanisms specific to a disorder.

To see the difference, consider Hacking’s perceptive study of the transient mental illness that came to be known as resignation syndrome. This mystifying condition occurred almost exclusively among child refugees in Sweden, who became despondent and apathetic to the point of turning mute and refusing to eat (some children required feeding tubes). Hacking explained the condition as a general trauma response interacting with highly local cultural variables. The children began to express their profound distress in new ways, which caught on via imitation; Swedish psychiatrists responded by crafting and broadcasting a new diagnosis, which covertly created a ‘script’ that children unconsciously internalised. The behaviours co-evolved, and stabilised each other. The children acquired a ‘new psychic state’ that was ‘not so easy to remove’.
Anorexia’s symptoms seem held in place by something more than just cultural scripts and general distress

This view gets quite close to social constructionism, as the bulk of explanation falls to cultural factors. Hacking thinks there are general psychological processes – trauma responses, social imitation and internalisation – that allow specific cultural content to create and sustain abnormal behaviours. But these processes are not quite NCMs. Internalisation, for example, is a general process by which behaviour that begins as a performance becomes real to the person doing it. An analogy Hacking uses, borrowed from the historian André LeBlanc, is hypnosis: subjects initially say they are just playing along, yet begin to find the instructions ‘more and more compelling’. Hacking does not think resignation syndrome involves an abnormal nor distinctive form of internalisation: it is just the same process as in hypnosis. As the philosopher Dominic Murphy argues in The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Medicine (2025), Hacking’s view requires ‘no distinctive machinery beyond that of ordinary cultural transmission and social learning’. The same explanations, he quips, could be offered ‘to show why my son and his friends are covered in tattoos’. It is in this sense that Hacking is a constructionist. There are no internal NCMs pulling strings, so there is no need for a science of abnormal minds, nor for treatments or classifications aimed at internal structures. The dynamics of socio-cultural shaping is, as Hacking puts it, ‘where the action is’.

Constructionism is plausible for resignation syndrome, and other conditions that are especially transient and culturally peculiar. But it does not adequately explain conditions like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which are highly heritable. What about conditions like depression, anxiety and anorexia?

Twin studies suggest that anorexia, too, is substantially heritable. So its symptoms seem held in place by something more than just cultural scripts and general distress. One interesting possibility is that patients systematically misperceive their own bodies: they literally see their figures as larger than they are. The source of these distorted perceptions would be an abnormal, scientifically tractable NCM – one we could use to improve classifications, explanations and treatments.

I think we can make progress by keeping NCMs in the picture, while exploring the possibility that culture can shape them too. What would it take for this view to be right? NCMs would need to satisfy two conditions: they would need to be appropriately plastic, and appropriately coupled to the cultural environment.

A mechanism is plastic if it can be reconfigured. Gold atoms are not plastic in this sense: change a gold atom’s structure and you no longer have gold, but some other element. Gold is fixed. In the biological and mind sciences, however, we find many plastic systems – especially those involved in adaptation, learning and regulation. For example, covering a kitten’s eye during a critical period of development reorganises its visual cortex. Neurons that used to respond to both eyes rewire to respond only to the open eye, and this persists even after the closed eye is reopened. Experience reconfigures the NCMs that allow kittens to see. Plasticity is a graded property: some systems are more stable across contexts and timescales, others more plastic.

But plasticity alone is insufficient. An NCM may be plastic but insulated from cultural inputs. The experiences that shape kittens’ visual systems are not cultural experiences. So coupling is a tougher condition to satisfy. We need the relevant NCMs to be responsive to cultural content.

Consider literacy. Reading is a cultural practice, only about 5,000 years old, too recent for evolution to have installed a specialised reading mechanism into the brain. Yet when people learn to read, even as adults, a patch of visual cortex that otherwise responds mainly to faces and objects becomes selectively tuned to written words. Here, cultural content shapes neural mechanisms: English and Hebrew readers’ brains become tuned to different letters, because their cultures write differently.
The uptake of emotion concepts and words – like ‘fear’ and ‘joy’ in a community – shapes those models

Literacy shows that cultural inputs can reorganise NCMs, in some cases. But are the mechanisms involved in mental disorders like this? Psychiatric disorders are vastly complex and difficult to study. So, it is helpful to find a simpler case study to test for plasticity and coupling. Emotion provides a case, and is especially relevant because many mental disorders are thought to be disorders of affect, motivation and emotion.

Affective scientists are split between two warring theories of emotion. On the one side are ‘basic emotion theorists’, such as the psychologist Paul Ekman who argues that a small set of basic emotions – including fear, anger, joy and disgust – are sculpted by evolution, cross-culturally stable, and powered by specialised neural circuits. In our terms, emotions depend on universal NCMs.

On the opposing side are ‘psychological constructionists’ (not to be confused with social constructionism) such as the neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett. Barrett argues that there are no dedicated circuits for emotions. Instead, brains build each emotion on the spot, by mixing general ingredients such as bodily signals, past experience and, most important here, concepts learned from one’s culture. Constructionists view the brain as continuously generating models of what to expect from the world and our bodies, and emotions emerge when incoming signals are unconsciously categorised according to those models. One striking claim is that the uptake of emotion concepts and words – like ‘fear’ and ‘joy’ in a community – shapes those models, and thereby shapes the mental and even physiological properties of emotions. This suggests a pathway through which cultural content can penetrate deep into the skull, and become entrenched in neural wiring.

That is, constructionists view even the paradigm ‘basic’ emotions as plastic and culturally coupled: emotion-mechanisms partly built by adaptation and learning satisfy plasticity; cultural factors causally shaping those mechanisms satisfy coupling. Constructionism thus predicts that people reared in different cultural environments have differently wired emotion systems, at least to some degree.

The emotion debate is far from settled. Constructionists are correct that emotional mechanisms appear far more variable and culturally idiosyncratic than basic emotion theorists predict. But conversely, emotions do seem to have pancultural characteristics: beta-blockers quell the racing heart and trembling hands of anxiety by blocking adrenaline’s effects on the body, and the brain circuits for learning fear are largely shared across mammals.

To settle the debate, we need more detailed data and experimental measures, but also better-differentiated theories. Presently, each theory can accommodate the same evidence. Basic emotion theorists explain cross-cultural similarities as the outputs of universal NCMs, and variations as culture modulating those outputs (similar to the illness/disease distinction). Psychological constructionists, by contrast, explain cross-cultural variations as the output of culturally varied NCMs, and explain similarities as similar cultural environments pushing those internal mechanisms to converge. This parallels the situation in psychiatry: we cannot settle debates about cultural shaping until our theories of brains, culture and mental disorders are better developed. Those debates turn on the degree to which the internal mechanisms of disorder are plastic and coupled.

Let’s briefly return to the case of anorexia in Hong Kong. If anorexia is appropriately plastic and coupled, then the Western anorexia script that arrived in 1994 may have done more than change how distress was expressed and experienced. It may have reshaped the NCMs that partly sustain its symptoms. That might warrant changes to how cross-cultural disorders are classified, explained and treated – perhaps as new subtypes, perhaps as new conditions. The anorexia Lee documented before 1994 and the anorexia he documented after may not be the same disorder after all.

In 2013, Thomas Insel, then director of the NIMH, gave a TED talk promoting the institute’s new commitment to biomedical explanations. He ended with an optimistic remark from Bill Gates: ‘We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years and underestimate the change that will occur in the next 10.’ Only four years later, however, Insel conceded that his 13 years spent spearheading research into the neuroscience and genetics of mental disorders, at a cost of some $20 billion, had produced plenty of interesting papers, but had not ‘moved the needle’ for patients. More than 10 years later, psychiatry has still failed to produce robust biomedical explanations of almost any mental disorder. (The clearest exceptions are DSM categories that reference known neurological diseases, such as ‘major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease’; other medical conditions, such as hypothyroidism producing a ‘depressive disorder due to another medical condition’; or substances, such as alcohol producing a ‘substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder’.)

Against sceptics, I don’t think this shows that biomedical-style explanations of mental disorders are wrongheaded. I do think this shows that biomedical frameworks cannot be easily transported from somatic medicine into psychiatry, because the crisp distinction between illness and disease may not hold for psychopathology. In that case, biomedical-style explanations need updating. If mental disorders are plastic and culturally coupled, then explanations must synthesise the insights of biological psychiatry and cognitive neuroscience with those of cultural anthropology and cross-cultural psychology. In turn, for social explanations to do informative work in psychiatry, they need to be made into testable hypotheses – especially those that can be hooked up to NCMs. Psychological constructionists offer a promising (albeit incomplete) way of doing this, by hypothesising rich social environments engaging equally rich and empirically tractable mechanisms.

If deep shaping is right, what does it imply about psychiatry? One implication is a ‘particularism’ about mental disorder. As Murphy puts it, this particularism predicts that neurological systems ‘are so shaped by cultural structures that we should expect to see psychological theories that do not generalise but obtain only within different human populations’. This does not entail that we abandon general classifications, or that we cannot identify scientifically useful kinds of disorders. But it does take seriously that disorders might be ‘local’: explanatorily stable only within certain cultural contexts. On such a view, the underlying mechanisms explaining anorexia or depression in China might be importantly different from those explaining their counterparts in the US. There is much work to do to develop this view, both theoretically and empirically.

Psychiatry should not uncritically accept universalism as its default assumption. It rests on an analogy with somatic medicine that may be premature. Deep shaping is a live and promising alternative hypothesis – one that avoids both overconfident claims of universalism, and the excesses of social constructionism.
